source.title: Learning the Language of the Microbiome with Transformers
source.authors: Neythen J. Treloar; S. ur-Rehman; Jenny Yang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Measures held-out autoregressive language-model evaluation loss across parameter sizes, using a scaling sweep in microbiome data; this is a direct measurement analogue in a new data domain.
record.gate_note: The study reports pretraining evaluation loss by model size, but does not report loss scaling against training tokens or compute, fit a power-law loss function, or test prediction of larger-run loss from smaller runs. Downstream benchmark scores are not pretraining-loss measurements. Detailed per-task and subset benchmark curves are not separately transcribed as numeric rows where the text gives only plotted values.
record.test_reason: The study trains GPT-2-style causal models from 6M to 170M parameters on microbiome taxon sequences. It reports held-out pretraining loss against model size (Fig 1A–B) and fine-tuned downstream scores against model size (Fig 5, S7). This is a new, non-text setting, so T3 rather than T1. No power-law fit, token or compute scaling, or extrapolation is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that pretraining improves downstream performance, that pretraining is a prerequisite for positive model scaling, and that pretrained representations transfer across biomes. They report that pretraining loss falls with model size (linearly in log size). They leave open why the 45M model, not the 170M model, scores best: possible causes are too little task data, a plateau, or noise.
record.recipe_differences: Uses GPT-2-style causal next-token prediction and held-out evaluation loss across model sizes, but on microbiome taxonomic-abundance sequences rather than natural-language text, with a different corpus, scale range, and training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream scaling differs with pretraining; task-wise scaling is variable. Early stopping affects reported final evaluation loss, and the authors note that smaller models may not have fully converged.

fits_no_version.finding: Non-pretrained transformers fine-tuned from random initialisation get worse, and vary more across replicates, as model size grows (Fig 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Without pretraining, scaling transformer size on small supervised datasets degrades downstream performance.

record.problems: The parameter sweep spans only roughly one order of magnitude; evaluation-loss values are plotted rather than tabulated, and no power-law fit or uncertainty estimates for those loss values are reported. Some models exited early, and the authors say smaller models may not have fully converged. Downstream scaling varies across tasks, and the 45M model scores highest on the aggregate benchmark rather than the largest model.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed model-by-task and pretraining-subset benchmark curves in Figures S7–S9 were not separately transcribed; their stated task-wise variability is captured in r13. They are downstream performance results rather than additional held-out pretraining-loss measurements.

untested.parts: Power-law form, which was not fitted (authors describe loss as linear in log size). Scaling in tokens or compute. Range beyond ~1.5 decades. Repeated data (training ran up to 100 epochs on ~56M tokens), which was not studied as a factor.
Shape at a fixed parameter count is tested only for head count at 6M and for the near-size 79M vs 85M pair. Wide ranges of depth and width are not tested.
Predictability from pretraining loss is not tested. Downstream scaling with pretraining data size is shown only indirectly (Fig 6).
No extrapolation from smaller to larger runs.
No compute-optimal allocation between parameters and tokens.

missing.what: Downstream score falls when pretraining data is subsampled to 110k (Fig 6D–E vs 6B–C). Also, 6M-MGM trained on 539k samples beats the original MGM trained on 260k, though this is confounded with tokenisation. Both bear on downstream improvement with pretraining-data scale.
Approximate min eval loss range read from the Fig 1B axis (~3.8 at 6M to ~3.2 at 170M), with the authors' description of the trend as linear in log size.

record.verdict_notes: Rows were relinked from V1 to V5 because the data are not natural-language text. The record's V4 limits_scope label was dropped: the parts of V4 it pointed to are untested, not shown to fail. Models were trained with early stopping rather than at matched compute or tokens, and the smaller models had not converged, so the loss-versus-size trend is not a clean parameter-bottleneck measurement.

versions.untested_parts: Tests evaluation loss against parameter count only. It does not test scaling against tokens or compute, bottleneck conditions, or a power-law fit over several orders of magnitude.
No extrapolation from smaller runs to larger runs is evaluated.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens is tested.
Only a comparison of two 6M models differing in attention-head count is reported; a wide range of architectures at fixed parameter count is not tested.
Tests microbiome taxonomic-sequence pretraining only. It does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling laws.
Reports downstream benchmark performance against parameter count, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss.
Does not compare fitting choices or compute-optimal splits, or test whether fitted exponents change with those choices.
